chapter_title: Introduction to AWS Monitoring with CloudWatch
chapter_summary:
Effective monitoring is the cornerstone of any robust cloud operation, and Amazon CloudWatch is the primary service AWS provides for this critical function. CloudWatch collects monitoring and operational data in the form of logs, metrics, and events, giving you a unified view of the health and performance of your AWS resources and applications. As a SysOps Administrator, your ability to interpret this data and configure appropriate alerts is paramount to maintaining system stability and performance. We begin by exploring the fundamental building blocks of CloudWatch: metrics. Metrics are time-ordered sets of data points that represent a variable being monitored. AWS services automatically publish a wealth of standard metrics to CloudWatch, such as CPU Utilization for EC2 instances, Read/Write IOPS for EBS volumes, or `Invocations` and `Errors` for Lambda functions. Each metric belongs to a namespace, which acts as a container for metrics from different services, preventing naming collisions. For example, `AWS/EC2` is a common namespace. Within a namespace, metrics are uniquely identified by their name and a set of dimensions—key-value pairs that provide additional context. For instance, `InstanceId` and `ImageId` are common dimensions for EC2 metrics, allowing you to filter and aggregate data for specific instances or groups.

While standard metrics offer broad visibility, real-world applications often require monitoring specific internal processes or custom performance indicators. This is where custom metrics come into play. You can publish your own application-specific metrics to CloudWatch using the AWS CLI, SDKs, or the CloudWatch Agent. Imagine you have a web application running on EC2 instances, and you want to track the number of failed login attempts or the duration of a specific database query. You can instrument your application code to emit these data points as custom metrics. When publishing custom metrics, you define the metric name, its value, a timestamp, and any relevant dimensions. It's crucial to choose meaningful dimensions that allow for flexible aggregation and filtering later. For example, a custom metric for login attempts might have a `Result` dimension (e.g., `SUCCESS`, `FAILURE`) and an `Application` dimension, allowing you to visualize failed logins per application. Remember that custom metrics incur charges, so plan your data collection wisely to avoid unnecessary costs.

Visualizing your metrics is just as important as collecting them. CloudWatch Dashboards provide a customizable home page in the CloudWatch console where you can monitor your resources in a single view. You can add various widgets to a dashboard, displaying line graphs for time-series data, stacked area charts, numbers for current values, or even text widgets for annotations. A well-designed dashboard offers a quick, at-a-glance overview of your system's health, allowing you to spot trends, identify anomalies, and correlate metrics from different services. For a SysOps Administrator, a common practice is to create dashboards tailored to specific operational roles or application stacks, ensuring that relevant information is always readily available. For instance, an "EC2 Performance" dashboard might show CPU, Memory, Network In/Out, and Disk IOPS for critical instances, while a "Web Tier Health" dashboard could aggregate metrics from your Load Balancers, Auto Scaling Groups, and application-specific custom metrics.

The true power of monitoring lies in its ability to alert you when something goes wrong, or is about to go wrong. CloudWatch Alarms enable you to watch a single metric over a specified period, and perform one or more actions based on the value of the metric relative to a threshold. When an alarm changes state (e.g., from `OK` to `ALARM`), it can trigger various actions, such as sending notifications via Amazon SNS, initiating an Auto Scaling action, or even executing an EC2 action like stopping or terminating an instance. When configuring an alarm, you define the metric to monitor, the period (e.g., 5 minutes), the statistic (e.g., `Average`, `Sum`, `Maximum`), the comparison operator (e.g., `GreaterThanThreshold`), and the threshold value itself. It's vital to choose appropriate thresholds that accurately reflect normal operating conditions and prevent both false positives (alarm flapping) and missed critical events. For example, an alarm on EC2 CPU utilization might be set to trigger if the average CPU exceeds 80% for 5 consecutive periods of 5 minutes. This `Datapoints to Alarm` setting helps prevent transient spikes from triggering unnecessary alerts. Always test your alarms thoroughly in a non-production environment to ensure they behave as expected and that notifications reach the intended recipients.

screens.title: Introduction to AWS Monitoring with CloudWatch
screens.subtitle: Understand metrics, dashboards, custom metrics, and alarms to keep AWS systems observable and reliable.

narration.text: Monitoring is how you know a system is healthy and how you detect problems early. In AWS, CloudWatch brings logs, metrics, and events into a single view so you can observe resource and application behavior. In this lesson you will learn what metrics are, how namespaces and dimensions give metrics context, when to publish custom metrics, how to design dashboards for rapid diagnosis, and how to configure alarms and notification actions. For example, you will see how standard EC2 metrics like CPUUtilization and EBS IOPS appear automatically, and how to publish a custom FailedLogins metric from an application. You will also learn practical alarm design: choosing a period and statistic, and avoiding false positives with datapoints-to-alarm settings. By the end of this chapter you will be able to collect meaningful telemetry, build a dashboard that surfaces critical signals, and set alarms that trigger the right actions. Think about what signal matters most in your environment and how you would know it’s degraded.

keyIdea.title: Why CloudWatch matters
keyIdea.text: CloudWatch unifies logs, metrics, and events to make system health observable and actionable; proper use prevents incidents and supports rapid diagnosis.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after completing this chapter

narration.text: These objectives set clear, practical goals for your CloudWatch skills. First, you will be able to explain the core purpose and capabilities of CloudWatch: how it collects logs, metrics, and events to provide operational visibility. Understanding this helps you choose the right telemetry to collect. Second, you will identify and interpret standard CloudWatch metrics for common AWS services so you can read trends and detect anomalies; a practical example is reading EC2 CPUUtilization and correlating it with network or disk input and output. Third, you will design and configure CloudWatch Dashboards that surface key signals for teams, arranging widgets to support quick triage. Fourth, you will learn to configure CloudWatch Alarms with appropriate thresholds and actions that notify teams or trigger automated responses. Each objective ties to a hands-on activity: launching an EC2, observing metrics, creating alarms, and validating notifications. Keep an eye out for common pitfalls, like alert flapping, and learn how period and datapoint settings influence alarm behavior. These skills together make monitoring effective and actionable.

screens.title: What is a CloudWatch Metric?
screens.subtitle: Definitions, examples, and why metrics are the foundation of monitoring

narration.text: A metric is a time-ordered set of data points that represents a variable you want to monitor. Metrics can be emitted automatically by AWS services or published manually as custom metrics. For example, an EC2 instance publishes CPUUtilization every minute; that time series lets you see patterns, spikes, and trends. Metrics are stored in namespaces, which isolate different sources—AWS services use namespaces like AWS/EC2, whereas you might create MyApplication for application metrics. Each metric is further qualified by dimensions, which are key-value pairs such as InstanceId or Application. Dimensions let you filter and aggregate, for example viewing C P U utilization for a single instance or an Auto Scaling group. A misconception to avoid is treating logs as metrics: logs record events with details, metrics summarize specific numeric values over time. Use logs for investigation and metrics for alerting and dashboards. In practice, choose metrics that are actionable: if a metric crosses a threshold, you should have a playbook or automated action ready. Consider cardinality when designing dimensions—too many unique dimension combinations increases storage and cost. What numeric signals in your system would you turn into metrics?

keyIdea.title: Metric = Time-series signal
keyIdea.text: Metrics are the numeric time series you will use to detect trends, trigger alarms, and drive dashboards.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › What is a Metric?
Definition
A time-ordered set of numeric data points representing a monitored variable, emitted by AWS services or custom sources.
Key points
  • Namespaces group metrics (e.g., AWS/EC2).
  • Dimensions add context (e.g., InstanceId, Application).
  • Choose actionable metrics to drive alerts and automation.
Key Takeaway
Metrics enable automated detection and concise dashboards. Pick metrics that lead to clear actions.
Example: EC2 CPUUtilization
EC2 publishes CPUUtilization under the AWS/EC2 namespace. Common dimensions include InstanceId and ImageId. You can graph the metric over time, apply statistics like Average or Maximum, and use it to trigger alarms when sustained high CPU is detected.
Metric anatomy
Namespace: AWS/EC2
Metric name: CPUUtilization
Dimension: InstanceId=i-0123456789
Common misconception
Logs are not metrics. Use logs to extract patterns and create metric filters when you need numeric counts from log lines.
Why it matters
Time-series metrics power automated alerts and dashboards that help you detect performance regressions and capacity issues before customers notice.

screens.title: Namespaces and Dimensions
screens.subtitle: How context is attached to a metric and why that matters for filtering and aggregation

narration.text: Namespaces act as containers for metrics and prevent naming collisions between services and applications. AWS services use namespaces such as AWS/EC2 or AWS/Lambda; you should use custom namespaces like MyApplication for your own telemetry. Within a namespace, metrics are identified by name and one or more dimensions. Dimensions are key-value pairs such as InstanceId, ImageId, Application, or Result. They give you the ability to scope a metric query to a specific instance, image, or app and to aggregate across dimensions when needed. For example, if you publish a FailedLogins metric with dimensions Application=WebApp1 and Result=FAILURE, you can graph failed logins for just WebApp1 or across all applications. A key design consideration is cardinality: avoid high-cardinality dimensions that produce too many unique metric series, as that increases cost and makes dashboards noisy. Also be deliberate with dimension design so alerts target meaningful groups. Finally, remember namespaces are the first level of organization and dimensions are the second; use both to make metrics queryable and actionable. Namespaces and Dimensions means namespaces group metrics by source and dimensions let you filter and aggregate so dashboards and alarms target the right scope.. In practical terms, how context is attached to a metric and why that matters for filtering and aggregation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Context matters
keyIdea.text: Namespaces group metrics by source and dimensions let you filter and aggregate so dashboards and alarms target the right scope.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Namespaces & Dimensions
Namespaces
Namespaces separate metric sources. AWS uses AWS/EC2, AWS/Lambda, and so on. Use a clear custom namespace for your application metrics to avoid confusion and to find your metrics easily in the console.
Example
Namespace: MyApplication
Metric name: FailedLogins
Dimensions: Application=WebApp1, Result=FAILURE
Design guidance
  • Keep namespaces meaningful and consistent.
  • Choose dimensions that allow useful aggregation without creating excessive cardinality.
  • Use dimensions to scope alarms and dashboard widgets precisely.
Dimensions example cards
InstanceId
Use to view a metric for a specific EC2 instance or to aggregate by instance.
Application
Group metrics by application or service name for team-focused dashboards.
Result
Use categorical values like SUCCESS/FAILURE to filter and count outcomes.
ImageId
Helps compare metrics across AMIs and identify version-related issues.
Common mistake
Using high-cardinality identifiers as dimensions (e.g., full request IDs) will create many time series and increase cost without useful aggregation.

screens.title: Standard Metrics by Service
screens.subtitle: Common CloudWatch metrics you will see from EC2, EBS, and Lambda

narration.text: AWS services publish a set of standard metrics that give you immediate visibility. For EC2, the most used metric is CPUUtilization, and you will also see NetworkIn, NetworkOut, and DiskReadOps/DiskWriteOps for EBS-backed drives. EBS volumes publish Read/Write IOPS and throughput metrics, which help diagnose storage bottlenecks. For Lambda functions, common metrics include Invocations, Errors, Duration, and Throttles; Duration helps identify slow functions and Errors indicate failed executions. Understanding these standard metrics helps you decide what to surface on dashboards and which metrics should have alarms. A common pitfall is selecting the wrong statistic: for example, using Maximum when Average is more representative, or vice versa. If an EC2 C P U has brief, extreme spikes, Maximum will reflect that, while Average smooths transient spikes. When building dashboards, choose the metric and statistic together. Also consider units and sampling period: not all metrics refresh at the same cadence. As you review metric names, think about what operational question each answers—capacity, latency, error rate—and let that guide alarms and dashboards. Standard Metrics by Service means know which standard metrics each aws service emits so you can monitor capacity, latency, and errors effectively.. In practical terms, common cloudwatch metrics you will see from ec2, ebs, and lambda. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Service signals
keyIdea.text: Know which standard metrics each AWS service emits so you can monitor capacity, latency, and errors effectively.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Standard Metrics
EC2
Key metrics: CPUUtilization, NetworkIn, NetworkOut, DiskReadOps, DiskWriteOps. Use these to track compute load, network throughput, and disk activity.
Use Average for steady trends; Maximum reveals brief spikes. Attach InstanceId as a dimension to scope by instance.
EBS
Key metrics: VolumeReadOps, VolumeWriteOps, VolumeReadBytes, VolumeWriteBytes, Throughput. These help identify storage I/O bottlenecks and sustained high latency scenarios.
Consider provisioning IOPS and monitoring burst credits for gp2 volumes; aggregate by VolumeId to focus on problem volumes.
Lambda
Key metrics: Invocations, Errors, Duration, Throttles. Duration helps you understand function latency; Errors indicate failed executions, and Throttles show concurrency limits being reached.
For latency-sensitive systems, create alarms on Duration p99 or on Errors to surface quality regressions early.
Practical tip
Map each metric to a question: Is the service overloaded? Is storage saturated? Is latency increasing? Let those questions define dashboards and alarms.

screens.title: Custom Metrics: When and How to Use Them
screens.subtitle: Deciding what to publish and designing dimensions for clarity

narration.text: Custom metrics let you capture application-level signals that standard metrics do not provide. Use custom metrics when you need to track business or internal technical events, like the number of failed logins, queue length, or a specific query duration. When designing custom metrics, choose a clear namespace and meaningful dimensions. For example, publish FailedLogins under the MyApplication namespace with dimensions Application=WebApp1 and Result=FAILURE so you can filter by application and outcome. Consider the cost: CloudWatch charges for custom metric storage and A P I calls, so avoid publishing overly frequent or highly granular metrics unless they are necessary. A practical process is: one, identify the operational question you want to answer; two, decide the metric name and unit; three, select a reasonable publish interval and dimensions; four, instrument code or use an agent to publish; and five, validate in the console and add to a dashboard. A common misconception is publishing everything you can: instead, publish metrics that lead to action, and consolidate noisy signals with sampling or aggregation. Which business signals in your application would justify a custom metric?

keyIdea.title: Publish with purpose
keyIdea.text: Custom metrics should answer operational or business questions; design them to be actionable and cost-aware.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Custom Metrics
When to create custom metrics
  • You need an application-level signal (e.g., FailedLogins).
  • You want to alert on a business metric or internal error count.
  • Log-based patterns should be counted and turned into metrics for alerting.
Design checklist
  1. Define the operational question.
  2. Choose metric name, unit, and publish interval.
  3. Select low-cardinality dimensions for useful aggregation.
  4. Estimate cost and tune frequency accordingly.
Concrete example
Track failed login attempts per application. Metric: FailedLogins, Namespace: MyApplication, Dimensions: Application=WebApp1, Result=FAILURE, Unit: Count. This allows alarm thresholds on failed login rates that indicate brute-force attempts or authentication regressions.
Common mistake
Publishing metrics at excessively high frequency or with high-cardinality dimensions, which makes queries noisy and increases cost without operational benefit.
Pro tip
If logs contain the signal, use CloudWatch Logs metric filters to convert matching log patterns into metrics instead of instrumenting every client path.

screens.title: Publishing Custom Metrics with CLI and Agent
screens.subtitle: Concrete commands and a sample workflow for EC2-based applications

narration.text: This screen shows how you publish custom metrics. The AWS CLI and CloudWatch Agent are common options. From an EC2 instance with the proper IAM role or configured credentials, you can use aws cloudwatch put-metric-data to publish a data point to a namespace. For example, to increment a FailedLogins metric, you provide the namespace, metric name, dimensions, value, and unit. The CloudWatch Agent can also collect system and application metrics and push them on a schedule. When using the CLI, ensure timestamps are correct and dimensions are meaningful. A misconception is expecting immediate dashboards: CloudWatch can take a few minutes to surface new custom namespaces and metrics. Also remember custom metrics incur costs; batch where practical. After publishing, verify in the CloudWatch console under All metrics and your namespace. Finally, add the new metric to a dashboard and create an alarm if you want notifications. Practice publishing a single event and watching it appear before automating frequent emits. Publishing Custom Metrics with CLI and Agent means use put-metric-data or the cloudwatch agent to publish custom metrics; verify in the console before automating frequent emits.. In practical terms, concrete commands and a sample workflow for ec2-based applications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Publish workflow
keyIdea.text: Use put-metric-data or the CloudWatch Agent to publish custom metrics; verify in the console before automating frequent emits.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › CLI & Agent
AWS CLI example
aws cloudwatch put-metric-data \ --namespace "MyApplication" \ --metric-name "FailedLogins" \ --dimensions InstanceId=i-0123456789,Application=WebApp1 \ --value 1 \ --unit Count
Replace the InstanceId placeholder with your instance ID. After running the command, wait a few minutes and check Metrics → All metrics → MyApplication in the CloudWatch console.
CloudWatch Agent
Install the CloudWatch Agent to collect system metrics and push metrics on a schedule. Use the agent for continuous metrics and the CLI for ad-hoc emits.
Validation & cost note
Verify the metric appears and is graphed. Custom metrics have costs, so batch emissions and choose sensible publish intervals. Use dimensions to avoid duplicate metric series.
Quick test
Publish a single data point and check the console before automating frequent publishes. This prevents accidental cost and cardinality issues.
Key Takeaway
CLI is ideal for ad-hoc metrics; the agent or SDKs are better for continuous telemetry. Always validate visibility and cardinality.

screens.title: Designing CloudWatch Dashboards
screens.subtitle: Widgets and layouts that make operational signals actionable

narration.text: Dashboards give teams a single view of critical metrics. Start by identifying the audience and the operational questions they need answered. For example, an EC2 Performance dashboard might include CPUUtilization, Memory (if available via agent), NetworkIn/Out, and Disk IOPS for critical instances. Use line graphs for trends, single-value widgets for current state, and stacked area charts when comparing multiple series. Arrange widgets so the most important indicators are prominent and group related widgets for a service or role. Text widgets help annotate deploys or incidents. Dashboards can combine standard and custom metrics and should focus on surfacing actionable anomalies rather than raw noise. Avoid overloading dashboards with every metric; instead create role-focused dashboards like Web Tier Health or Database Operations. Dashboards also support time range controls and annotation to correlate events with metric changes. Regularly review dashboards with stakeholders to ensure they reflect evolving priorities and reduce cognitive load during incident response. Designing CloudWatch Dashboards means build role-focused dashboards that answer specific operational questions and surface actionable anomalies.. In practical terms, widgets and layouts that make operational signals actionable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Dashboard design
keyIdea.text: Build role-focused dashboards that answer specific operational questions and surface actionable anomalies.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Dashboards
EC2 Performance — Example Widget Set
Top: line chart for CPUUtilization (Average). Middle: numeric widgets for current network in/out. Bottom: stacked area for Disk IOPS across volumes. Use consistent time windows for comparison.
Single Value
Current CPU % to quickly see if an instance is overloaded.
Text
Deployment notes or runbook links for on-call engineers.
Alarm Status
A widget showing counts of alarms in ALARM state for the stack.
Design checklist
  • Define the viewer and their top questions.
  • Choose 4–6 critical widgets; avoid overcrowding.
  • Use consistent time ranges to compare signals.
  • Annotate deployments and incidents for correlation.
Key Takeaway
Dashboards are for rapid diagnosis—surface the few metrics that answer critical operational questions for your team.

screens.title: CloudWatch Alarms: How They Work
screens.subtitle: Setting periods, statistics, thresholds, and datapoints-to-alarm

narration.text: A CloudWatch Alarm monitors a single metric and evaluates it against a threshold using a chosen statistic and period. You define the metric, the evaluation period (for example 5 minutes), and the statistic to use—Average, Sum, Maximum, Minimum, or SampleCount. The alarm compares the statistic to a threshold with an operator like GreaterThanThreshold. Datapoints-to-alarm is an important setting: it controls how many of the most recent periods must breach the threshold before the alarm transitions to ALARM. For example, setting Period to 300 seconds and Datapoints to Alarm to 3 out of 5 will require three of the last five five-minute periods to exceed the threshold. This reduces false positives from short spikes. A common misconception is using 1-out-of-1 for production alarms; that causes flapping. Always test alarms in non-production first and pick values reflecting sustained problems. Also ensure the alarm's statistic matches the operational question: use Average to smooth noise or Maximum to detect spikes. End by thinking: what duration of bad behavior should trigger an alert in your system? CloudWatch Alarms: How They Work means alarms evaluate a metric's statistic over configured periods. datapoints-to-alarm prevents transient spikes from triggering alerts.. In practical terms, setting periods, statistics, thresholds, and datapoints-to-alarm. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Alarm evaluation
keyIdea.text: Alarms evaluate a metric's statistic over configured periods. Datapoints-to-alarm prevents transient spikes from triggering alerts.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Alarms
Alarm settings explained
Metric: the series to watch. Period: evaluation interval in seconds. Statistic: Average, Sum, Maximum, etc. Threshold: the numeric value to compare. Datapoints-to-alarm: number of breached periods required for state change.
Period
E.g., 300s smooths short spikes.
Statistic
Choose Average vs Maximum based on the problem you want to detect.
Concrete example
Alarm: CPUUtilization > 80%. Period: 300 seconds. Statistic: Average. Datapoints-to-alarm: 3 of 5. This means sustained high CPU for about 15 minutes triggers the alarm, reducing false positives from transient spikes.
Common mistake
Using short periods with 1 out of 1 datapoints for production alarms causes flapping and alert fatigue.

screens.title: Alarm Actions and SNS Notifications
screens.subtitle: Connecting alarms to notifications and automated responses

narration.text: When an alarm changes state, CloudWatch can perform actions. The most common action is sending a notification via Amazon SNS, which distributes messages to email, SMS, or HTTP endpoints. Alarms can also trigger Auto Scaling or EC2 actions like stop or terminate. To set up an SNS action, create an SNS topic, add subscriptions such as an email address, and confirm the subscription. Then attach the SNS topic to the alarm's In alarm action. A useful practice is to separate test and production topics so noise in testing does not reach on-call teams. Also ensure permissions are configured so CloudWatch can publish to the SNS topic. A misconception is assuming all recipients will receive messages immediately; subscribers must confirm, and some delivery can be delayed. For automated remediation, consider safety and test thoroughly: an alarm that terminates an instance could cause data loss if misconfigured. Finally, document notification routing and runbooks so alert recipients know next steps when they receive an SNS message. Alarm Actions and SNS Notifications means use sns for human notifications and attach automated actions carefully; separate test and prod to avoid noisy alerts causing remediation errors.. In practical terms, connecting alarms to notifications and automated responses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Actionable alerts
keyIdea.text: Use SNS for human notifications and attach automated actions carefully; separate test and prod to avoid noisy alerts causing remediation errors.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Alarm Actions & SNS
Step 1
Create an SNS topic and add subscriptions (email, SMS, HTTP). Confirm subscriptions before attaching to alarms.
Step 2
Create or edit the CloudWatch alarm and add the SNS topic as the In alarm action.
Step 3
Test the alarm in a non-production environment. Use separate SNS topics for test and production to avoid noisy production alerts.
Automated actions and safety
Auto Scaling actions can be triggered by alarms, and alarms can stop or terminate instances. Because these are destructive, protect production by testing and adding safeguards like lifecycle hooks or review gates.
Permission note
Ensure CloudWatch has permission to publish to the SNS topic and the topic allows the necessary principals to subscribe and receive messages.

screens.title: Avoiding Alarm Flapping — Best Practices
screens.subtitle: Choosing period, statistic, and datapoints-to-alarm to reduce false positives

narration.text: Alarm flapping happens when transient metric spikes repeatedly change an alarm between OK and ALARM, creating noise and reducing trust. The most effective mitigation is adjusting the evaluation period and datapoints-to-alarm. Increase the period to smooth short spikes—common production settings use 300 seconds—and require multiple breached datapoints like 3 of 5 to ensure sustained problems are reported. Also choose the right statistic: Average smooths short spikes, while Maximum catches brief extremes. Another tactic is to use composite alarms to combine multiple signals so a single noisy metric does not trigger an alert by itself. For testing, it is tempting to set Datapoints-to-Alarm to 1 out of 1 to see immediate results, but remember to revert to production-safe values later. Finally, document expected normal ranges and runbooks for alarm responders. The assessment scenario in this chapter demonstrates these principles: increasing period to 5 minutes and setting 3 out of 5 datapoints avoids false positives while still alerting on sustained high C P U. How would you tune alarms for a bursty but resilient workload? keyIdea.title: Reduce noise
keyIdea.text: Use longer periods, multiple datapoints, appropriate statistics, and composite alarms to prevent flapping and preserve signal quality.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Avoid Alarm Flapping
Tuning recipe
  1. Choose a period that smooths transient noise (e.g., 300s).
  2. Select a statistic matching the problem: Average for sustained issues, Maximum to detect spikes.
  3. Set Datapoints-to-Alarm so multiple periods must breach before alerting (e.g., 3 of 5).
  4. Test in non-production and observe alarm behavior before deploying to production.
Assessment example
The recommended change to reduce flapping is to increase the Period to 5 minutes and set Datapoints to Alarm to 3 out of 5, so the alarm reflects sustained high CPU rather than brief spikes.
Additional strategies
  • Use composite alarms to require multiple independent signals.
  • Annotate dashboards with deploy times to correlate metric changes.
  • Document runbooks so responders know the expected actions for each alarm.
Key Takeaway
Tune alarms for sustained problems, not transient noise. Proper tuning preserves trust and reduces operational churn.

narration.text: These are the core ideas to hold onto. First, metrics are time-ordered numeric series and are the primary signals for alerting and dashboards. Second, namespaces and dimensions provide context—namespaces group metrics by source, and dimensions let you filter and aggregate the series you need. Third, custom metrics capture application-level signals that standard metrics do not, but they must be designed to be actionable and cost-aware. Keep these points in mind as you build dashboards and alarms: choose metrics that answer operational questions, design dimensions to be useful and low-cardinality, and validate everything in a non-production environment. Finally, tune alarms to detect sustained problems by choosing appropriate periods and datapoints-to-alarm settings. These fundamentals make monitoring reliable, reduce noise, and enable faster incident response.
